confidence: Low to moderate about motives; low about culprit. Nearly everyone now has a grievance and concealed misconduct, so motive alone has weak discriminating value. Arrival statements and all admissions remain testimony, not guaranteed truth.
plausibility_notes: Accepted rival job gives Artie a meaningful counterweight to a previously dominant motive. Death before donation may hurt Monet's planned payroll repair, complicating her incentive credibly.
Dada owning the warning is a satisfying correction to an easy activist stereotype. Its artistic interpretation fits the text while leaving room for suspicion.

Specific confessions have distinct professional content, but thirty consecutive polished admissions of hidden wrongdoing plus donor retaliation make Grant seem omniscient and the room improbably synchronized.
The repeated structure of confession, Grant's threat and sardonic closing analogy becomes conspicuous. Nearly every person sounds equally articulate under homicide questioning.
Hugh, Tess, Anya and Ella append exact first-admission times to motive speeches. These feel planted as access exclusions, especially because the timing is unprompted and only some people supply it.

Monet, Dada, Paige and Brie mention shelves or room use before discussing motives. These disconnected openings feel like clues inserted to secure later access logic rather than natural conversational transitions.
Thirty suspects each owning a separate offense creates breadth but dilutes emotional contrast; a few ordinary frightened or uncertain responses would feel more human.
Institutional corners cut under donor pressure are believable individually. Their cumulative scale risks making the museum itself comically negligent, which may fit party tone but weakens naturalism.
No innocent-truth rule exists. I will treat job acceptance and arrival claims as provisional rather than mechanically clearing speakers.
